title: From the right–privilege distinction to claims of entitlement
shortTitle: From the right–privilege distinction to claims of entitlement
summary: A protected property interest may arise from law or a sufficiently binding understanding that limits official discretion over a benefit; personal importance alone does not establish it.
notes:
The older right–privilege approach treated government employment and benefits as discretionary largesse outside ordinary due-process protection. The assigned Bailey discussion illustrates that view. Cafeteria Workers rejected a categorical answer based solely on the absence of a right to a particular government job, although its contextual analysis upheld the limited exclusion from a military installation. Greene separately illustrates how a severe impact on work opportunities influenced interpretation of the authority to revoke a security clearance.

Charles Reich’s New Property argument urged protection of government-created economic relationships central to modern liberty and security. Roth subsequently required identification of a legitimate claim of entitlement grounded in an independent legal source, such as state law or binding understandings. Perry confirms that a formal written tenure clause is one possible source, while established institutional practices and mutually explicit understandings may also qualify. A subjective expectation alone does not.

The doctrine distinguishes the source of substantive security from the constitutional adequacy of procedures for taking it away. It also leaves separate constitutional restrictions in place: a government employer may violate free-speech rights by retaliatory nonrenewal even where the claimant lacks a property entitlement to renewal.
